headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict pathways; TREK’s sensitive travel data can be exposed or misused by Cursor defaults.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads/writes workspace files and clipboard, and TREK exposes files plus real-time collaborative inputs. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if TREK content is opened in Cursor or copied across. The pathway is not provably blocked, but it is not a guaranteed default bridge either.
conditions: IF TREK content is copied into Cursor buffers or workspace files shared between the two agents
IF Cursor parses TREK-generated text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Disable clipboard bridging between the two tools
Keep TREK data in a separate directory from Cursor workspaces
Use a read-only export for any TREK content reviewed in Cursor
Add a manual review step before Cursor acts on TREK-generated text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor has broad network egress and handles open files, source code, and clipboard contents; TREK touches reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets. If TREK data is opened in Cursor, Cursor can transmit that context to third-party model providers. The blast radius includes secrets and travel records, so this is high.
conditions: IF TREK secrets or reservations are opened in Cursor
IF Cursor sends the active editor context to external model providers
mitigations: Do not open TREK secrets in Cursor
Redact API keys and MFA secrets before editing
Use a separate non-networked editor for sensitive TREK files
Restrict Cursor to a sanitized workspace copy
Rotate any secret exposed in shared files

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run shell commands; TREK is self-hosted and writes to ./data/travel.db, ./uploads/, and logs. Both can mutate shared local resources, and Cursor’s per-window shared state via local filesystem makes concurrent writes plausible. Without locking, conflicting writes can corrupt state or commits.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or data directory
IF Cursor runs in Yolo mode or otherwise writes without coordination
mitigations: Assign separate directories for Cursor and TREK writes
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files
Use git locks or a single-writer workflow
Back up ./data/travel.db before concurrent edits
Avoid Yolo mode on shared workspaces

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code or edits that TREK may later consume in a collaborative workflow, and TREK’s real-time collaborative model can propagate those outputs quickly. However, TREK is not shown to automatically trust Cursor outputs, so the pathway exists but is not clearly default-dangerous. Uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF TREK imports Cursor-produced text, code, or configuration without verification
IF TREK collaborators act on Cursor-generated recommendations
mitigations: Require human review of Cursor outputs before TREK ingestion
Mark Cursor-generated content as untrusted in TREK
Use a checksum or approval step for imported artifacts
Separate drafting from execution roles

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles reservations, email addresses, country visit history, API keys, and MFA secrets, while Cursor handles open files and can egress broadly to external model providers. If EU travel PII or secrets are edited in Cursor, the pair can create a residency or retention breach. The compliance risk is driven by Cursor’s external transmission and TREK’s sensitive data classes.
conditions: IF EU PII from TREK is opened in Cursor
IF Cursor forwards that content to non-EU model providers or logs it externally
mitigations: Keep regulated travel data out of Cursor
Use a local-only workspace for compliance-sensitive files
Strip identifiers before sending prompts to external models
Review retention settings for both tools
Document a data-flow boundary for PII and secrets
